title: Plato's Just City
objective: After this level you can explain why Plato's Republic argues for rule by philosopher-kings and how his three-class city mirrors a just soul.
summary: Plato’s ship of state argues that philosophers, who know the Good and don’t want power, should rule a just city where each class does its own work; Popper called it totalitarian.

cards.headline: Would you let the passengers vote on who flies the plane?
cards.body: Plato thought steering a city takes expert knowledge, just like steering a ship. From that one thought he built an entire ideal city, and a very odd idea of who should run it.

cards.headline: The ship of state
cards.body: In Plato’s Republic, Socrates pictures a ship. Its sailors quarrel over the helm, though none has learned navigation, and they mock the one person who studies the stars and winds as a useless stargazer. The point: ruling takes knowledge, and a crowd may not recognize it. So Socrates says cities will have no rest from their evils until philosophers become kings, or kings take up philosophy.

cards.headline: Three classes, three parts of you
cards.body: The ideal city has three classes: ruling guardians, auxiliaries who defend it, and producers who make what it needs. Your soul, Plato says, has three parts too: reason, spirit and appetite. A city is just when each class does its own work, and a person is just when each part does, with reason in charge. Justice is a well-run team, inside you and out.

cards.headline: Power for people who don’t want it
cards.body: Why trust philosophers? They are educated to know the Forms, above all the Form of the Good. And they’d rather study than rule, so they must be compelled to take their turn. Socrates turns that into a rule of thumb: the city whose rulers are most reluctant to govern is always the best and most quietly governed.

cards.headline: Popper’s charge
cards.body: In 1945 Karl Popper charged that the Republic is totalitarian: its rulers aim at the unity of the city as a whole, whatever citizens want for themselves. Defenders reply that, for Socrates, a ruler’s whole task is to benefit the ruled. Readers still argue over which picture of Plato’s city is fair.

cards.headline: Plato’s Just City: the big picture
learned: Ship of state: ruling needs knowledge
Three classes, three parts of the soul
Justice: each part doing its own work

questions.prompt: In Plato’s Republic, what makes a city just?

options.label: Each class does its own work
Every citizen votes on each new law
options.rationale: Plato didn’t want rule by the crowd.

options.label: All property is divided equally
options.rationale: Justice is about each class’s work.

questions.explanation: A city is just when its guardians, auxiliaries and producers each do their own work, as the soul’s parts should.

questions.prompt: Why does Plato’s ship parable suggest philosophers should rule?

options.label: Philosophers are the strongest people aboard
options.rationale: The parable is about knowledge, not strength.

options.label: Ships were the main source of Athens’s wealth
options.rationale: The ship is a picture of the city.

options.label: The sailors had elected their captain fairly
options.rationale: The sailors seize the helm by quarrelling.

questions.explanation: The sailors know nothing of navigation yet mock the true pilot; ruling a city, like steering, needs knowledge.

questions.prompt: Plato’s rulers are trained to know the Forms. According to Level 4, how are Forms known?

options.label: Through the senses, by touch
options.rationale: The senses show only imperfect copies.

options.label: Through thought rather than the senses
Through messages from the gods
options.rationale: Plato says we grasp them by thought.

questions.explanation: For Plato the Forms, including the Form of the Good, are grasped by thought, not by the senses.
